iti hi nirūpitam | tatra saṃketasya smaraṇaṃ saṃskārādhānasaṃskāraprabodhayorāyattam, tau ca nirvikalpakena kartumaśakyau | uktaṃ hi anubhavaḥ paṭīyān smṛtibījamādhatte, tādṛśadarśanādasya prabodhaḥ iti | paṭīyastāṃ ca anubhavasya na aparāṃ kāṃcana manmahe ṛte vimarśaviśrānteḥ | yadapi bhaṭṭena nirūpitaṃ praroho'syāḥ paṭīyastvam .......................... | (page 221) iti | tatrāpi prarohasya pramātṛviśrāntimahamitthameva bhāse- ityevaṃbhūtavimarśarūpāṃ tāṃ kimutānyadrūpāmutpaśyāmaḥ | tādṛśatvamapi darśanasya prarūḍhataiveti vimarśarūpatvābhāve kathaṃ saṃskārasya ādhānaṃ prabodhanaṃ vā syāt | yat punaḥ prāmāṇyaparīkṣāyai bhaṭṭena uktaṃ vyaktaḥ [vyarthaḥ prakāśaḥ ga. |] prakāśaḥ svārthārthaṃ [svārthārthasaṃ kha. |] saṃskārapratibodhakaḥ | nānyathā syādvikalpe'pi tatpravṛttirapīṣyatām || iti | tatra yadi vyaktiḥ prakāśasya yathāvyākṛtaprarohapaṭīyastvādirūpā na iṣyate, tadā na kiṃcit | apaṭīyaso'pi ca saṃskāraprabodhakatvāpattīḥ | paṭīyānitiviśeṣaṇānarthakyaṃ kīrtigranthe | yaśca tatra viniścayaḥ saṃvāditaḥ taddṛṣṭāveva dṛṣṭeṣu saṃvitsāmarthyabhāvinā | ityādiḥ, tatra saṃvidaḥ sāmarthyamasāmarthyavilakṣaṇamastyeveti alaṃ bhūyasā | etadeva krameṇa nidarśayati nahi iti | agnitvameva hi dhūmahetutvamiti dṛṣṭe vahnau tat dṛṣṭameveti nālikeradvīpavāsino'pi tathā saṃskārādhānāt bhavet smaraṇam | dhūmaheturayamiti smaraṇalakṣaṇakāryābhāve ca kāryaikānumeyaḥ saṃskāra āhita iti kathaṃ bhavet | evaṃ saṃskārasya ādhānaṃ vimarśaśūnyo bodho na karotīti nidarśya prabodhanamapi na karotīti nidarśayati nāpi dhūmaḥ iti | nanu kāraṇatvamarthasya paropādhikatvena vyavahāraparaṃ [hāryaṃ paraṃ ga. pāṭhaḥ |] na sākṣātkāramanupādhikasvalakṣaṇaprakāśanamātrasvabhāvamupā- roḍhumalaṃ, tat kāraṇatvaṃ dṛṣṭameva netyāśaṅkya nidarśanāntaraṃ darśayati mārgagamana iti | nacāpi iti pūrveṇa saṃbandhaḥ | svātmani iti ādhānābhāvasya udāharaṇam, sahacāri ityādi prabodhanābhāvasya | evamupasaṃharati tataśca iti | vimarśarūpatātmakakāraṇābhāvāt (page 222) tatkāryasaṃskā
**Memory's seed and the "this jar" are the reflexive-awareness** The reflexive-awareness is the source of the powers. Now Abhinavagupta shows that even the *impression* — the seed of memory — is nothing without it. How does a memory get laid down, and how does it awaken? The schools would say: the experience lays a trace, and the later seeing of something like it awakens the trace. But Abhinavagupta presses: what makes the experience strong enough to lay the seed? It is the resting of the experience in the reflexive-awareness — the moment in which the experience is aware of itself, "I, thus, shine." Without that self-awareness, the experience would be an inert flash; it could not lay a seed, nor could it be awakened. The non-construction, the bare sensory flash, cannot do it. The Bhaṭṭa had said the strength of the experience is what lays the seed. But even this strength, Abhinavagupta replies, is the resting in the knower — the reflexive-awareness. If the light's manifestation, its being-strong, is not admitted, then nothing at all would lay a seed; and the not-strong would have to be the awakener too, making the whole "strong" distinction meaningless. The point is driven home with the smoke-and-fire example. "Fire-ness itself is the smoke-cause-ness" — we see this in the fire. If the mere impression, without the vimarśa, laid the memory, then even the coconut-island dweller, who has never seen smoke, would remember fire from smoke. But he does not. Without the vimarśa-form cause, the impression is neither laid nor awakened — just as the smoke does not awaken the fire-memory in one who never knew fire. And this is the deeper point: the very act by which we take the world — the determination (adhyavasāya) — is itself the reflexive-awareness. When we say "this jar," the determination "this jar" is not a mere name-and-form, a word pasted onto a thing. It is, Abhinavagupta declares in kārikā 20, *beyond* name and form: it is the param-Lord's power, manifesting like the self, not by the this-ness. The "this" of the jar is not something the jar has from outside; it is the Lord's own reflexive-awareness, shining through the act of determination. The vācya-vācaka (the signified and the signifier), the sphoṭa — all these analyses fail, because the "this-ness" they try to locate in the word or the thing is really the self's own manifestation. So memory and determination are both the reflexive-awareness. The impression is laid and awakened only by the vimarśa; and the determination "this jar," far from being a word pasted on a thing, is the param-Lord's power manifesting like the self. The vimarśa is not one power among others; it is the very form of the light, present in the memory's seed, in the determination's "this," and in every act by which the self knows and takes its world. ---

> The claim is that the essence of light is the reflexive awareness, not the bare showing of objects. > The crystal supplies the contrast: a light that merely showed the world without knowing that it showed > it would be no different from crystal — it would reflect, but be inert. What makes the light conscious > is the self-awareness in the very act of manifesting. The passage then identifies this self-knowing > with the supreme speech (parā-vāk) and with the Lord's freedom and lordship. > > The identification with the Word is the extension: the reflexivity is not a bare self-presence but > the supreme speech from which the lower levels of language descend. This is why the word-joined "I" > need not be a construction — language is the form the self-grasp takes, not something that produces > it. The passage establishes the reflexivity claim; the full account of the powers and the Lordship is > developed in the following vimarśas. parā-vāk (supreme speech) · svātantrya/aiśvarya (freedom/lordship).
